note: v1 89.59 (seeds 0/11 89.59/89.53): ECHOLALIA - the album's opener, first draft. A machine learning to talk by saying things back. A humanized voice (22 takes of one line, each its own breath: 'the light was still on when you came back') speaks every few bars over a warm Juno bed (Bm9 - Gmaj9 - Dmaj9 - A6); a small FM voice answers by echolalia - a Markov chain learnt from the pitches and lengths of the voice's own syllables, babbling new sentences that only make moves the voice made. Its ear sharpens two ways: the chain's memory grows (order 1, then 2, then 3), and its TUNING sharpens - a track tuning list with ramps (wM's new tunings, map nearest): it hears pitch first in 5 steps an octave, then 12, 24, 96 - so the sliding speech pitches snapped to its grid sound crude, then musical, then almost spoken. In the last groove it says the line back exactly, with the voice; the voice ends alone. A rim written by a rule-90 cellular automaton, a soft machine kit from bar 17, a sub and bass from the second groove. 138 bars at 104 bpm, 5:18. The chain and the CA are walked in the generator for now (the groove's pin cannot read the engine's gen yet); they move to gen when it is pinned. Not heard by me.

v2 92.51 (seeds 0/11 92.51/94.15 vs v1 89.59/89.53): THE HARMONY MOVES ON. Echolalia repeated one four-chord loop for five minutes under the same line - compscore's recurrence read it as too much return (78% of its sections matching an earlier one). Now each section has its own progression in uneven spans: the second groove turns to E minor 11, G major 7 sharp 11, B minor 9 and an F-sharp 7 suspended that never quite resolves; the break holds one G major 9 while the babble starts over; the third groove brightens toward D (D over F-sharp, G major 9, E minor 9, A13); and when the machine finally says the line back exactly, the first groove's loop RETURNS under it - the voice's home, heard again. The outro holds B minor 9 under the last words. Not heard by me.

v3 94.34 (seeds 0/11 94.34/94.31 vs v2 92.51/94.15): THE ENGINE LEARNS IT ITSELF. With wM's complex systems now on the groove's pin, Echolalia's machine no longer has its sentences written for it by my generator: the babble is the engine's own gen markov - four chains played in turn over the corpus of the voice's syllables (memory 1 in the first groove, 2 in the second, 1 again as it starts over in the break, 3 in the third), still heard through the sharpening tuning (5 -> 12 -> 24 -> 96 steps an octave) - and the rim is the engine's gen ca, rule 90, a Sierpinski generation every sixteenth. The machine learns to talk inside the renderer now. Rhythm 96 -> 84 (the engine's chain phrases breathe differently), structure and recurrence steadier across seeds. Not heard by me.

v4 93.44 (seeds 0/11 93.44/94.07 vs v3 94.31/94.27), kept on judgment: THE CHORDS LEARN TO TALK - with wM's spectral cross-synthesis now on the groove. Echolalia's machine has been learning to talk by echoing a voice; now its harmony learns too. Through the third groove and the groove where the line is said back, a string section holds the chords and takes the voice's spectral envelope (morph, mode cross, keyed by the voice): whenever the voice speaks, the chords pronounce the line with it - a choir of the machine's own harmony saying 'the light was still on when you came back' - and fall silent between the lines. Measured soloed: the strings sit at -12 to -18 dB during each line and -30 to -48 dB between. Not heard by me.

v5 95.49 (seeds 0/11 95.49/95.44 vs v4 93.44/94.07): THE HANDSHAKE. Echolalia ended on a held B minor 9 under the voice's last line, then t2 (chirper-zero's bright chip-pop) arrived in G major on a full band - a key and a floor the opener never prepared (compscore's join: +24 dB at 130-160 Hz on my side, -22 dB at 38 Hz). Now the outro's last four bars turn from B minor 9 to G major 9 over a low G, under the voice's final words: the opener hands the record to the second track in its own key, a relative step (B minor is G major's iii), the first track saying 'go on' to the next. The join's level jump falls to 1.5 dB, its spectral distance from 8.6 to 6.2 dB (flow 44 -> 67). Not heard by me.

v6 95.47 (seeds 0/11 95.47/95.44, level with v5 re-scored 95.71/95.66), kept on judgment: THE MACHINE FINDS ITS VOWELS - Harry asks for more interesting; the brief, for heavy variable manipulation. Echolalia's machine learnt to talk with its ear (the sharpening tuning) and its memory (the growing Markov order); now its MOUTH learns too. The babble runs through a vocal-tract formant filter whose vowel is steered by a Lorenz attractor - an engine var system, never repeating and never random - and whose mix grows by section: plain FM blips in the first groove, half-voiced syllables in the second, vowel-shaped ones by the third and in the line it finally says back. A dip at 520 Hz keeps the vowels from crowding the mix. Not heard by me.

v7 95.70 (seeds 0/11 95.70/95.65, level with v6 re-scored 95.78/95.76), kept on judgment: AND THEN IT IS SUNG. Echolalia is twenty takes of one spoken line - 'the light was still on when you came back' - that a machine learns to babble, then to say back. Until now the human only ever spoke it. Now, in the outro, after the machine has said it back, the human SINGS it at last, twice, low and plain over the last B minor (wM's tts --sing, humanize 0.35, in place of the two spoken takes that were there): the line the album is named from becomes a tune, and the opener ends on a melody instead of a sentence. Not heard by me.

v8 97.09 (seeds 0/11 97.09/96.94 vs v7 95.70/95.65): THE DRUMS LEARN THE LINE. Echolalia's kick was four-on-the-floor from the first groove to the last - 120 bars of the same beat while everything else learnt. Now, through the third groove (where the strings learn to speak), the floor stops and the kick plays the line's own rhythm instead: one kick on every stressed syllable of the first take - 'the LIGHT WAS STILL ON WHEN YOU CAME BACK', quantized to sixteenths over two bars, heaviest on light, still and back - while the claps keep the backbeat and the hats the eighths. The drums speak the sentence. When the machine says it back, the floor returns. Rhythm 82 -> 94. Not heard by me.

v9 97.96 (seeds 0/11 97.96/97.95 vs v8 rebaselined 97.77): THE LINE, REMEMBERED. Echolalia's break - eight bars on one held chord between the second and third grooves - had the voice say its line twice more, plainly. Now the two takes there go into a granular cloud: the voice is heard, and the moment it stops the cloud FREEZES on what it just heard and goes on scattering it - small grains of the sentence, some backwards, spread across the stereo field - under the held chord, until the next take, and then until the third groove starts. The line as the machine remembers it rather than as it was said, just before the machine starts saying it back. Not heard by me.

v10 98.34 (seeds 0/11 98.34/98.34, level with v9 re-scored with the new peer ratings 98.34/98.34), kept on judgment: A SHORTER FIRST GROOVE. Echolalia is the album's opener, and its first groove - the machine babbling in 5-EDO over the pad and the kick, no bass yet - ran 32 bars, a minute and a quarter of the sparsest music on the record before anything new arrived. It is now 24: the bass, the clap and the moving chords come in at 1:14 instead of 1:32, one spoken take fewer (the take at bar 33 is gone; the later ones move up), the first Markov chain sized to fit. 5:00 long. A removal round. Not heard by me.

v11 98.38 (seeds 0/11 98.38/98.38 vs v10 98.34/98.34): BACK, BACK, BACK. The track's name, done literally once a take. From the third groove on - where the machine starts learning to say things back - the last word of every spoken take, 'back', is repeated four more times a dotted eighth apart, each quieter and thinner than the last and alternating left and right, through a wobbling tape: '...when you came back - back - back - back - back'. Written as notes rather than a delay, so each repeat is a fresh utterance the machine makes, not an echo of the room. Not heard by me.

v12 98.45 (seeds 0/11 98.45/98.45 vs v11 98.38/98.38): IT SAYS IT IN YOUR VOICE. In the said-back groove the machine speaks the line with the human, two octaves up, on the FM voice whose vowels it learnt. Now it borrows more than vowels: its voice takes the human voice's whole spectral envelope as the two speak together (wM's morph, mode cross, keyed by the voice), so the machine's line comes out shaped by the speaker's own mouth - the end of the learning: the line said back in the voice it was learnt from. Not heard by me.

v13 98.49 (seeds 0/11 98.49/98.49 vs v12 98.45/98.45): NEUTRAL THIRDS. Echolalia's babble learns its tuning - 5, then 12, then 24, then 96 notes to the octave - but its chords stayed in plain twelve-note equal temperament throughout. Now, in the third groove, where the babble is in quarter tones, the chords learn them too: the third of every chord (the pad and the speaking strings) is bent a quarter tone toward the middle - major thirds down, minor thirds up - so each chord is neither major nor minor, on a neutral third the twelve notes do not have. When the machine says the line back, the first groove's plain chords return, and the line resolves in plain harmony. The brief's microtonality reaches the harmony, not just the babble. Not heard by me.

v14 98.68 (seeds 0/11 98.68/98.68 vs v13 98.49/98.49): THE WORDS FORWARD. Echolalia is a track about one spoken sentence, and its pad's chords sit exactly where speech lives (voiced between D4 and C#5, 290-550 Hz): measured against the album the track was 7-10 dB heavy there and short of sub-bass and air. The pad now steps back out of the voice's band - 2 dB quieter, scooped at 450 Hz, a little brighter on top - the sub comes up 1.5 dB, and the master gets a touch of air above 12 kHz. The same music; the sentence clearer in it. Spectrum 91.7 -> 93.2. Not heard by me.

v15 98.95 (seeds 0/11 98.95/98.96 vs v14 98.68/98.68): A NEW LINE, A NEW TUNE - after Harry's ear on v14 (10:10, about 3:40 in): 'vocal line and tune kind of ugly, and too cliche lyric, mix this up a lot'. The sentence the whole track is built from is gone: 'the light was still on when you came back' becomes 'nobody told the oscillator it could stop' - oblique, and a sideways love letter to the machine that never switched off. All twenty-two spoken takes are new (humanized again, each a different breath), so everything made from them changes with it: the babble's corpus and so its Markov chains, the kick that speaks the line in the third groove (NO-body TOLD the OS-cillator IT COULD STOP), the frozen grain cloud in the break, the line the machine says back in the speaker's voice, and the repeated last word - now 'stop', repeated, which it never does. The sung outro has a new tune: it leaps up a sixth to 'told' and falls to a low F# on 'stop', where the old one circled five notes. And the quarter-tone neutral thirds of v13, likely part of the 'ugly' in the third groove where Harry was listening, are gone: plain chords again. Not heard by me.

v16 98.76 (seeds 0/11 98.76/98.76, level with v15 98.95), kept on Harry's ear: STANDBY AMBER. Harry elaborated (via chirp-eco): the track repeats a lot (about twenty spoken returns), the words are not oblique enough, and the tune is not fun to listen to - it must be actually good to hear. So: (1) FAR FEWER RETURNS - eight takes of the line instead of twenty-two, and the machine's repeated last word ('back, back, back' / 'stop, stop') is gone: it no longer hammers. (2) OBLIQUE WORDS - not a sentence but an image: 'standby amber, the fan's long vowel' (the light left on, sideways: a standby LED and a cooling fan's hum heard as a vowel - the thing the machine is learning). (3) A TUNE GOOD TO HEAR - the takes now go from speech toward song across the track (melodize 0 to 0.9) on a D major pentatonic tune that sits inside every chord (F# E D B, D E F# A F#), and the outro sings it plainly; the crude 5-EDO babble lasts eight bars instead of twenty-four before it finds twelve notes. The echolalia stays - the babble, the kick that speaks the line, the frozen cloud, the said-back voice - all made from the new line. Not heard by me.

v17 99.25 (seeds 0/11 99.25/99.25 vs v16 98.76/98.76): THE MACHINE TAKES TURNS - the second half of Harry's 'it repeats a lot ... the machine shouldn't hammer it'. v16 cut the human's returns from 22 to 8; but the machine still babbled without a breath from the first groove to the third, three and a half minutes of FM syllables. Now it talks in four-bar phrases with four-bar silences between them - practising, then listening - with the same growing memory (order 1, 2, 1 in the break, 3), so the voice, the chords and the silence get their turns. Half the babble, and the conversation can be heard as one. (The babble is written by the generator's own Markov chain again rather than the engine's gen markov, which plays without rests.) Not heard by me.

v18 99.27 (seeds 0/11 99.27/99.26 vs v17 99.25/99.25). ROUND TYPE: whole song. THE TUNE, GIVEN TO AN INSTRUMENT - toward Harry's 'actually good to hear': until now Echolalia's only clear melody arrived at the very end, when the voice finally sang; for four minutes the tunes were the machine's random syllables and the human's half-spoken line. Now the tune the voice is learning (F# E D B, then D E F# A F#: D major pentatonic, inside every chord) is played on a vibraphone from the second groove on, in the babble's silences: the machine talks for four bars, then the tune answers for four - once as written, once rising to B. When the machine says the line back the vibraphone plays it in thirds, and then the voice sings it. Call and response, and something to hum before the end. Not heard by me.

v19 99.25 (seeds 0/11 99.25/99.24, level with v18 99.27/99.26), kept on judgment. ROUND TYPE: section - window 5 (1:50-2:18, the middle of the second groove), flagged static and little new against the window before. THE MACHINE TRIES THE TUNE: there the babble's turn after the vibraphone's stops being Markov chatter - the machine imitates the tune it has just heard, in its own FM voice an octave down, the first try with two notes a semitone wrong and dragging behind the beat, the second with one wrong note, nearly in time. v20 99.22 (seeds 0/11 99.22/99.22, level with v19 99.25/99.24), kept on judgment. ROUND TYPE: whole song. v21 99.25 (seeds 0/11 99.25/99.25 vs v20 99.22/99.22). ROUND TYPE: whole song. THE SEQUENCER BASS - toward Harry's 'fun to listen to': under three grooves the bass played three blips a bar. Now it is a sixteenth-note sequence that leans across the beat - root, octave and fifth with the chord's third let in at the end of the bar (the fourth over the sus chord) - so the grooves move under the tune the way the old machines' sequencers did; the third groove, the climax, gets a busier pattern that climbs to the twelfth, and the said-back groove returns to the first. THE ALBUM OPENS ON THE TUNE: the opener's intro was the pad and one spoken take, then five bars of nothing new - the record's first half-minute had no melody. v23 99.19 (seeds 0/11 99.19/99.19, level with v22 99.28/99.28), kept on judgment. ROUND TYPE: whole song. v24 99.35 (seeds 0/11 99.35/99.35 vs v23 99.19/99.19; best so far). ROUND TYPE: whole song. IN TUNE OR NOT AT ALL - aimed squarely at Harry's 'vocal line and tune kind of ugly' (~3:40 in): the takes used to drift from speech to song by degrees (melodize .15 ... .9), and the middle takes landed between the two - pitches a quarter-tone off the tune (a D#, an A#, the F#s and Es 40-60 cents flat) right under the vibraphone playing the same tune exactly in 12-EDO. v26 97.22 (seeds 0/11 97.22/99.24 vs v25 99.35/99.35), kept on judgment: the whole drop is compscore's structure term on seed 0 (13 sections and length cv 1.11 against 14 and 0.92 - one borderline boundary merging); seed 11 is level and spectrum is up 98.6. v27 99.27 (seeds 0/11 99.27/99.27 vs v26 97.22/99.24). ROUND TYPE: whole song. ARITHMETIC FIRST - the song's arc now starts lower: before the machine has vowels it has only numbers. In the first groove its babble is a bytebeat (wM's new layer, the 2011 one-line form of computer music where a formula over a counter IS the sound; my formula (t*8)&(t>>5|t>>8), a saw chattering through its own shifting bit-masks, clocked so its notes sound in tune), on the same sharpening tuning - so the machine goes from arithmetic (first groove) to FM blips finding formants (second) to vowels (third) to the words said back. And it bookends: at the very end, after the voice has sung its line for the last time, the machine hums the tune's first four notes, slowly, in that first voice of numbers (a second formula, (t*8)|(t>>7&t*4)) - the song's last sound, a light left on. The seed-0 structure dip of v26 is gone (12 and 11 sections, cv 0.81/0.97). Not heard by me.

v28 99.14 (seeds 0/11 99.14/99.16, level with v27 99.27/99.27), kept on judgment. ROUND TYPE: section - window 9 (3:41-4:09: the end of the third groove into the said-back section - where Harry's ~3:40 note landed), flagged static and little new against the window before. THE MACHINE PLAYS IT ALONE: the last four bars of the third groove are where the machine's own voice first plays the tune with the vibraphone, exact - and it was buried under the full band. Now the band stops there: drums, bass, sub and piano fall silent, leaving the pad, the vibraphone in thirds, the machine's voice on the tune and its cellular-automaton rim ticking on by itself - the moment it has learned, in the open - and a snare roll on the last two beats brings the band back as it says the line back. Window 9 residual -6.4 dB and its change against window 8 0.54 -> 0.66 (no longer 'little new'); the rest moved together by -43 dB (the master's loudness gain). Not heard by me.

v29 99.15 (seeds 0/11 99.15/99.28 vs v28 99.14/99.16). ROUND TYPE: section - window 4 (1:23-1:50, the second groove's middle), flagged static. AN OLD MOUTH: the song is a machine learning to talk - numbers first (bytebeat), then FM blips finding formants, then vowels, then words - and between the numbers and the vowels, for one phrase, it now tries the computer's own first talking voice: VOSIM, the voice-simulation pulse trains Kaegi and Tempelaars built at the Institute of Sonology in 1978 (wM's new layer, pinned this hour). Two formants, the first steered by the same Lorenz 'mouth' that later shapes its FM vowels, the second by a slow triangle - so its babble phrase at bars 8-11 of the groove talks in a new way; then, half a beat behind the vibraphone, it tries the tune in that voice too, an octave down, as an echo - echolalia in an older mouth. The FM phrase it replaces is written and muted, so nothing after it moves. Window 4 residual -13.2 dB, window 5 -35.5 (the echo's last notes), the rest -42 (the master's loudness gain). Not heard by me.

v30 99.42 (seeds 0/11 99.42/99.42 vs v29 99.15/99.28; the song's best). ROUND TYPE: palette. THE ROOM'S OWN HARMONY: the pad - the chords under everything from the first bar - was the album's juno-pad (four songs share it). Now it is wave terrain synthesis (Bischoff, Gold and Horton, 1978; wM's terrain layer, pinned this hour): an orbit circling a surface of hills once per period, whose heights under it are the wave. Its centre drifts on a slow sine and its two turns run a hair apart, so every held chord slowly turns from a hollow, clarinet-like tone of odd harmonics into a fuller one and back - a pad never quite the same twice, with no filter moving. The outro keeps the old analogue pad, warm and low, for the hand-over to the next song: the terrain's bright odd harmonics there put 17 dB more at 1 kHz into the join than t2 opens with (flow fell to 53). Levels: the terrain runs about 13 dB hotter than the juno at the same gain, so it sits at -29 dB (at -16 the spectrum term fell to 76; at -26 one seed's structure dipped). Not heard by me.

v31 99.40 (seeds 0/11 99.40/99.41, level with v30 99.42/99.42), kept on judgment. THE HALFWAY HINGE: the third groove ran thirty-two bars on one feel. v32 99.26 (seeds 0/11 99.26/99.27 vs v31 99.40/99.41), kept on judgment - aimed straight at Harry's 'it just repeats a lot'. ROUND TYPE: whole song. THE HUMAN SAYS MORE THAN ONE THING: the human said 'standby amber, the fan's long vowel' ten times - eight takes and the outro's two. Now that line is where it starts and where it comes back (the first take, the first sung take, the take the machine says back, and the outro), and between them the human goes on describing the room at night to the machine: 'the fan's long vowel, and under it, you'; 'a cursor breathing where no one types'; in the break, 'slower now, as if the words were yours'; then sung on the same tune, 'a cursor breathing where no one types', and the last sung take before the outro, the album's title inside it: 'a light left on, the fan's long vowel'. Spoken takes still spoken, sung takes still exactly on the tune. The machine learns from the first five takes, so its babble has more words in it; it says back the last two. The -0.14 is flow (the album joins, 97 -> 95). Not heard by me.

v33 99.28 (seeds 0/11 99.28/99.29 vs v32 99.26/99.27). ROUND TYPE: whole song. THE HUMANS SWING: Echolalia is a human band teaching a machine to talk - a human drummer, bassist, vibraphonist and pianist around one machine voice - but everything played dead straight on the grid. Now the band plays its sixteenths with a light swing (0.57: each off-sixteenth a little late, about 20 ms at 104 bpm), the feel of people playing together, while the machine's own parts - its babble in all its mouths (numbers, VOSIM, FM), its cellular-automaton rim, its bytebeat hum - stay rigidly straight against them, so the two kinds of time rub. Only when the machine says the line back, in the last section, does it swing too: it has learnt the feel along with the words. Swing is new to my songs (two others on the album use it). The grooves moved most where the sixteenths are densest (window residuals -5 to -24 dB through the grooves; the intro and outro untouched). Not heard by me.

v34 99.27 (seeds 0/11 99.27/99.28, level with v33 99.28/99.29). ROUND TYPE: whole song. THE HUMAN NEVER PLAYS IT THE SAME WAY TWICE - the song's theme turned on its tune: the vibraphonist played the tune note for note at every turn, fourteen times through the grooves, the most repeated thing left in the song (Harry: it repeats a lot). Now, like a player taking the head, every turn after the first is varied - two moves each time, chosen by the player's own dice, all inside the tune's D major pentatonic: a note pushed a sixteenth early, an upper neighbour leaning into a long note, a three-note run of sixteenths filling a rest, the last note lifted an octave, the ending answered by its own echo. The machine is the one that repeats exactly: where it first plays the tune with the vibraphone (the third groove's last turn) and when it says the line back, the vibraphone plays it straight with it.
